title: Discovery of apoE4 modulators for Alzheimer’s disease therapy
text:
The ε4 allele of the apolipoprotein E (APOE) gene is the strongest genetic risk factor for Alzheimer disease.
ApoE4 exacerbates not only amyloid pathology but also tau-mediated neurodegeneration. Our proposal seeks
to identify small molecule apoE4 inhibitors, thereby reducing apoE4-related pathogenic effects for AD therapy.

title: Orbitrap Astral MS Instrument
text:
Revolutions in mass spectrometry technology have broken through prior imitations in
sensitivity allowing for the analysis of 10,000-15,000 proteins from 150 ng of protein. In
addition, ultra fast acquisition speeds and high resolution data independent acquisition will
enable identiﬁcation and quantiﬁcation of post-translational modiﬁcations important for
understanding cellular signaling. The acquisition of the Orbitrap Astral will provide cutting
edge technology in sensitivity and detection for proteomic expression and structural biology
projects accelerating biomarker and drug discovery efforts.

title: Single cell multi-omics approaches in identifying driving cells and genes in pediatric MODS patients requiring ECMO support
text: (See instructions): This NIH R00 proposal seeks support for developing an independent research program to gain a deeper understanding of the cellular and molecular mechanisms associated with MODS deterioration, who may require advanced life support. My long-term goal is to develop innovative diagnostic and therapeutic methods for pediatric diseases in the intensive care unit (ICU), using cutting-edge single-cell multi-omics techniques and machine learning approaches. My previous research focused on identifying novel drugs, biomarkers, prognostic, and diagnostic markers for various diseases and cancers using big data approaches. However, MODS in pediatric patients with veno-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) support has drawn my attention, as the survival rate for severe MODS patients with ECMO support is very low and there are no clinical or molecular biomarkers available to diagnose deterioration of MODS patients requiring ECMO support. To gain a deeper understanding of the cellular and molecular mechanisms associated with MODS deterioration, who may require advanced life support, I aim to utilize advanced single-cell multi-omics and machine learning approaches. My previous research using bulk RNA-seq analysis on a small sample size showed that dysregulation of the immune response and epigenetic variations are significant factors associated with MODS deterioration in patients requiring ECMO support. However, a more detailed analysis using advanced single-cell multi-omics and machine learning is needed. The objective of this award is to use cutting-edge single-cell multi-omics techniques to investigate the cellular heterogeneity and their dynamics, as well as their transcriptional regulatory elements in MODS and ECMO patients at two different time points. Furthermore, a machine learning approach along with bulk RNA-seq will be implemented to identify crucial cells and genes associated with MODS patients' deterioration who may require ECMO support. The successful completion of this research will expand my knowledge in single-cell multi-omics, statistics, machine learning approaches, immune responses, and pediatric diseases.

title: Pathogenesis of Immune checkpoint inhibitors-induced myocarditis
text:
Immune checkpoint inhibitor-associated myocarditis (ICI-myocarditis) is a highly fatal disease occurring in cancer
patients, but the mechanism, pathogenesis, and risk factors are understudied. We propose that tissue resident
T cells autoreactive to myosin (Myhc-specific TRM) drive the development of ICI-myocarditis and that targeting
Myhc-specific TRM can prevent the development of ICI-myocarditis. This study is highly translational and can
directly impact our understanding of the pathogenesis and risk factors of ICI-myocarditis, and designing new
therapeutic strategies.

title: Molecular mechanisms of Ras and Receptor Tyrosine Kinase Convergence on PI3K in cancer
text:
Phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) alpha, a crucial lipid kinase, catalyzes the conversion of PIP2 to PIP3 at the
cell membrane, initiating signaling cascades governing cellular growth, proliferation, and survival. Despite the
prevalence of activating mutations in PI3K alpha across diverse human cancers, their mechanistic underpinnings
remain elusive, hampering therapeutic interventions targeting PI3K. This proposal integrates structural studies
using cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM), enzymology and native mass spectrometry to investigate how
activation of PI3K is orchestrated by key upstream signals: activated Ras and Receptor Tyrosine Kinases, and
how disease mutations interfere with these mechanisms leading to cancer.

title: Identification of novel osmosensing receptors in C. elegans
text:
The ability to sense osmolarity changes is vital for human health, and robust mechanisms are evolved to keep
the osmolarity of body fluids within a narrow range. The knowledge gap in the molecular identities of
osmosensors has greatly hindered our understanding of osmoregulation mechanisms. The proposed work
aims to identify the first osmosensors in the animal kingdom, providing novel insights into the mechanisms of
osmosensation, osmoregulation and related diseases.

title: Real time relapse risk scoring for Opioid Use Disorder (OUD) from clinical trial datasets
text:
Clinicians who treat patients with OUD collect standardized clinical data such as urine toxicology and self-
report of use of substances, as well as medication dosing and clinic treatment engagement. Nevertheless, it is
currently not possible to predict, in real time, what the risk is for a patient to relapse in the next week or month.
This project aims to apply well developed contemporary statistical and machine learning methodologies to
build such a relapse risk score, which would be of benefit to both clinicians and researchers.

title: Underdiagnosis of primary immunodeficiency disorders: Recognize and Educate
text: Knowledge generated from the proposed research will provide an evidence base for addressing disparities in the diagnosis of primary immune deficiency (PID). Because early diagnosis and treatment of PID are crucial for the prevention of permanent organ damage and death, addressing disparities in PID diagnosis will have a significant public health impact and is relevant to NIMHD’s mission to reduce health disparities.

title: AI-assisted quantitative photon-counting-detector CT imaging for cytogenetic risk prediction and treatment response in multiple myeloma
text:
This project will develop a new low-dose CT imaging technique to quantitatively identify response to multiple
myeloma therapy, stratify cytogenetic risk, and provide prognostic models, which will guide treatment choices.
In the long-term this project will establish CT imaging as a noninvasive pathway to measures changes in the
activity of multiple myeloma disease after therapy and eliminate the need for routine invasive bone marrow
biopsies.

title: Programming multi-pronged immune response to glioblastoma with IL-13Ra2/TGF-b CAR-T cell therapy.
text:
We aim to develop effective immunotherapy for glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) by deploying IL-13Rα2/TGF-β
bispecific chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cells that can both (a) directly target GBM through IL-13Rα2
surface-antigen recognition and (b) modify the tumor microenvironment by converting TGF-β from an
immunosuppressant into a stimulant of engineered CAR-T cells. We will evaluate the ability of IL-13Rα2/TGF-β
CAR-T cells to directly eliminate IL-13Rα2+ GBM, as well as to induce endogenous immunity against IL-13Rα2–
GBM, in both patient-derived orthotopic xenograft models and immunocompetent mouse models. This work will
rigorously evaluate the safety and toxicity profile of IL-13Rα2/TGF-β CAR-T cell therapy, and generate
comprehensive preclinical data in support of a phase-1 clinical trial for the treatment of patients with GBM.

title: Mutations and Target Genes in Adenoid Cystic Carcinoma
text:
Adenoid Cystic Carcinoma (ACC) is a slow-growing salivary gland tumor that is treated by surgery and
radiation, often leaving patients disfigured and with significant morbidity. Many ACC patients survive more than
10 years after the standard therapy of surgery and radiation, but a fraction succumb much more quickly and
others acquire distant metastases or relapse 5 or more years after the initial treatment. This project will use
detailed RNA sequencing analyses to learn more about the biology of ACC tumors, to identify the patients at
highest risk of relapse and to translate our findings to clinical laboratories so the information can be
successfully used to help patients.

title: MOSAIC: Imaging Human Tissue State Dynamics In Vivo
text:
PROJECT 2: IMAGING THE DYNAMIC TISSUE STATE IN PATIENTS IN VIVO 
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) measures many different physical properties of the tissue which may be 
correlated with the specific tumor behavior (e.g., proliferation, inflammation, angiogenesis) found in the limited 
biopsies available per patient. This project will fuse readily available MRI to spatially localized biopsies to build 
predictive models of cellular composition across the unsampled tumor (and brain) to track and validate cell 
composition changes to standard and immune therapies. Connecting these imaging changes to patient survival 
will allow identification of clinically beneficial shifts in cellular cohabitation.

title: Repeat enhancers as drivers of ETV6-RUNX1+ and ETV6-RUNX1-like B-lymphoblastic leukemia
text:
The proposed research is relevant to public health because ETV6-RUNX1+ B-lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL)
is one of the most common cancers of children, requiring many months to years of intensive therapy for cure,
with some patients relapsing and dying. Understanding the fundamental driver mechanisms that sustain
malignancy in this cancer and a rarer but more aggressive subtype, ETV6-RUNX1-like B-ALL, could lead to less
toxic therapies.

title: Training Program in Big Data Systems Neuroscience
text:
Research in neuroscience is crucial for attacking the causes of neurological and mental health
disorders. If the field of neuroscience is to continue its rapid advance, neuroscientists must use,
understand, and develop new technologies, acquire and analyze ever larger data sets, and
grapple more directly with the complexity of neurobiological systems. The primary goal of this
training program will be to help train the next generation of systems neuroscientists with the
experimental and computational skills needed to make the discoveries of tomorrow.

title: Mechanistic studies of chromatin modification in transcription regulation
text:
Many tumor types are characterized by altered patterns chemical tags found on the histone proteins that
package the human genome, leading to defects in gene regulation and DNA repair. Insights into the molecular
mechanism by which cells attach and remove these tags, as well as how the tags regulate gene expression,
can be used to devise new treatments. This research is being used to drive efforts to develop drugs to treat
cancers that are resistant to current therapies.

title: Role of vascular smooth muscle cell-enriched lncRNA in atherosclerosis
text:
The project will study the function and mechanism of the long noncoding RNA PRDM16-DT, which is highly
expressed in vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs) and lies within an atherosclerosis risk locus of unknown
function. Defining how PRDM16-DT regulates VSMC phenotypes and atherosclerosis development will advance
understanding of vascular disease mechanisms and may guide the development of new VSMC-based gene
therapies for atherosclerosis.

title: Trpc5-activated neural circuits and maternal behavior
text:
We discovered that loss-of-function mutations affecting the TRPC5 gene (encoding a calcium channel) can
impair maternal behavior. Here we will further unravel the neurobiological mechanisms by which the Trpc5
channel maintains normal maternal behavior during the postpartum period, and will provide pre-clinical evidence
to identify Trpc5 as a potential target to improve maternal behavior.

title: Defining the Role of Retinal Microglia and Infiltrating Monocytes on Photoreceptor Cell Death in Retinal Detachment
text:
Retinal detachment is an ocular emergency that can lead to permanent blindness due to photoreceptor cell
death. Detachment of the retina can occur in all ages, from newborns to adults, and is characterized by active
infiltration and activation of local microglia and peripheral monocyte/macrophages. Through the successful
execution of this proposal, we will gain new mechanistic insights to effectively target these populations and
develop novel neuroprotective strategies to prevent vision loss.

title: Molecular and Functional Evaluation of NOTCH1 Deficient iPSC Derived Cardiomyocytes in Hypoplastic Left Heart Syndrome
text:
Patients with congenital heart disease (CHD) are the fastest growing population of adults in the world. While
patients with severe forms of CHD are surviving into adulthood, they face a disproportionate burden of
arrhythmias and heart failure that leads to their morbidity and mortality, the cause of which is unknown.

title: CRISPR Screens to Reveal Key Regulators of Radiation-Induced Cardiovascular Injury
text:
Radiation therapy can save lives by treating cancer but often damages the heart, increasing the risk of heart
disease in cancer survivors and astronauts exposed to radiation. This research will uncover the genes and
pathways that cause radiation-related heart injury and develop new strategies to protect heart health and improve
long-term survival.
